title: Wine law and labels
lead: How the big wine countries rank and protect their wines, the US labeling percentages, and how to read what a label is telling you.

intro.title: TWO EU TIERS, MANY NAMES
intro.text: In Europe, protected wine sits in two EU tiers. Each country uses its own words for them.

tiers.name: PDO / DOP / AOP
tiers.note: France AOC/AOP, Italy DOCG and DOC, Spain DO and DOCa, Germany Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein

tiers.name: PGI / IGP
tiers.note: France IGP, Italy IGT, Spain Vino de la Tierra

sections.name: Old World, New World

lines.label: Three label styles
lines.text: Wines are labeled by grape, by region, or by a made-up name. Old World countries mostly label by region. The region's law decides which grapes go in.

lines.label: What the terms mean
lines.text: Old World means the countries where modern winemaking traditions began, like France and Italy. New World means countries that borrowed them, like the US, Australia and Chile.

know: A Chablis label says Chablis, not Chardonnay.
Made-up names are often blends that break a region's rules, like the first Super Tuscans.
Old World style tends to be lighter, lower in alcohol and higher in acid; this is typical, not a rule.
The exam asks you to read grape, color and style from a label.

visuals.title: Three ways a wine is labeled

items.name: By name

sections.name: France: AOC, AOP and IGP

lines.label: AOP
lines.text: Every production step happens in one defined area, by known methods. The rules sit in a 'cahier des charges' approved by the EU.

lines.label: AOC and IGP
lines.text: AOC is the national step before EU registration as AOP; wines may still print AOC. IGP links a wine to its origin; for wine, harvest to finished wine happens in the zone.

know: AOP is the EU sign; AOC is the French national equivalent.
Only wine may keep using the term AOC.
INAO has run France's origin system since 1935.
IGP wines are also checked by state-certified bodies.

sections.name: Italy: DOCG, DOC and IGT

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Italy splits its DOP wines into DOCG and DOC. IGT is Italy's word for IGP. A DOCG must have been a DOC for at least seven years.

lines.label: Label words
lines.text: Classico means the oldest zone. Riserva means extra aging. Superiore means lower yields and more alcohol.

know: DOCG rules must be stricter than the DOC they came from.
Riserva: at least two years for reds, one year for whites.
Gran Selezione is only for DOCG wines from the estate's own grapes.
DO wines must show a vintage, except fortified, non-vintage sparkling and frizzante.

sections.name: Spain: DO, DOCa and Pago

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Vino de la Tierra is Spain's IGP. DO needs prestige and five years as a quality region. DOCa needs ten years as a DO and bottling inside the zone.

lines.label: Aging words
lines.text: Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva climb in minimum aging. Level 1 needs the order, not the exact times.

know: Rioja is a DOCa.
Vino de Pago is a DOP from one site with its own soil and microclimate.
Under Spanish law, red Crianza needs 24 months, 6 in oak.
Rioja's own rules are longer: Crianza 2 years with 1 in oak.

rows.name: DOCa
rows.note: 10+ years as DO, bottled in zone

items.name: Reserva
items.text: 3 years, 1 in oak, 6 months in bottle

sections.name: Germany: the Prädikat levels

lines.label: The tiers
lines.text: Deutscher Wein has no named origin. Landwein is regional. Qualitätswein comes from one of 13 regions. Prädikatswein is Qualitätswein graded by ripeness at harvest.

lines.label: Ripeness, not sweetness
lines.text: Riper grapes earn a higher Prädikat. The winemaker still decides how sweet the wine ends up, so Kabinett and Spätlese can be dry.

know: Prädikatswein may not be chaptalized.
Eiswein: as ripe as Beerenauslese, picked frozen at minus 7°C or colder.
The 1971 law made ripeness at harvest the main quality measure.
Grosses Gewächs is a dry single-vineyard top wine (a VDP term, now also in the 2021 law).

visuals.title: The six Prädikate, least to most ripe

sections.name: United States: AVAs and percentages

lines.label: AVA
lines.text: An American Viticultural Area is a defined growing region with a name, its own features and a set boundary.

lines.label: The numbers
lines.text: Name a grape: 75%. Name a state or county: 75%. Name an AVA: 85%. Name a vineyard: 95%. A vintage with an AVA: 95%.

know: A vintage with a state or county appellation needs 85%; with an AVA, 95%.
'Estate bottled' needs an AVA and grapes grown on the winery's own or controlled land.
Naming two or more grapes means listing each percentage.
Showing a vintage or grape name means the label must show an appellation.
The Court lists Oregon at 90% for most varietals and 95% for AVAs.

visuals.title: US federal minimums
visuals.note: TTB rules, 27 CFR part 4. Vintage with a non-AVA appellation: 85%.

sections.name: Reading a label

lines.label: Five parts
lines.text: Producer, region, grape or appellation, vintage, and alcohol. If no grape is named, the appellation's rules tell you what's inside.

lines.label: Watch for
lines.text: Estate bottling has its own phrase in each language. 'Reserve' and 'Old Vines' have no official meaning in many places.

know: Chablis = Chardonnay, Chianti = Sangiovese, even though the label won't say so.
NV means non-vintage, a blend of years.
Mis en bouteille au château/domaine is French for estate bottled.
Imbottigliato all'origine is the Italian equivalent.

visuals.title: What to find on any label

mixups.why: AOP is the EU-wide protection; AOC is France's national step before it, still allowed on wine labels.
DOCG sits above DOC, needs 7+ years as a DOC and stricter rules.
DOCa needs 10+ years as a DO and bottling inside the zone; Rioja and Priorat are DOCa.
85% of the grapes must come from the AVA; 95% must come from the stated year.

sources: INAO, Italian Law 238/2016, Spain's Ley 6/2015 (BOE), Consejo Regulador DOCa Rioja, Wines of Germany (DWI), TTB and 27 CFR part 4 (eCFR), and the Court of Master Sommeliers Americas curriculum guide, with Wine Folly as a labelled secondary source. Checked Oct 31, 2026.

facts.fact: Introductory exam content: wine law of important regions (connecting grapes with places or appellations, and appellations with styles) and reading a wine label (determining grape variety, color and style from the label).
Section 3 of the Introductory course outline is 'Understanding Wine Law'.
Regional wine laws dictate which grape varieties can be grown and how they are grown in many wine regions.
Wines are labeled in one of three ways: by grape variety, by region, or by a made-up name.
Labeling by region is used mostly in Old World countries such as France, Italy, Spain and Portugal; each region dictates which grapes may be used (e.g. Chablis is Chardonnay, Chianti is Sangiovese).
Named (made-up) wines are often blends that don't fit a region's wine law; Tuscan wines with French grapes such as Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet gave rise to the first Super Tuscans.
Wine Folly's varietal minimums: 75% USA (Oregon 90%), 80% Argentina, 85% for Italy, France, Germany, Austria, Portugal, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and the UK.

'Old World' refers to traditional winemaking countries such as France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Germany; 'New World' refers to countries that borrowed those traditions, e.g. North and South America, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand.

Old World wine tends to have lighter body, lower alcohol, higher acidity and less fruit; New World wine tends toward fuller body, higher alcohol, lower acidity and pronounced fruit. These are typical, not rules.

Five basic parts of a label: producer or name, region, variety or appellation, vintage or non-vintage (NV), alcohol by volume. NV wines can pull wine from multiple vintages. 'Old Vines' has no rule for how old the vines must be.
A Chablis label does not mention Chardonnay; an appellation wine relies on the appellation's rules to tell you what's in the bottle.
Estate-bottled terms: Mis en bouteille au château / au domaine (France), Imbottigliato all'origine (Italy), Erzeugerabfüllung (Germany).
'Reserve' on a label has no official meaning (Wine Folly); the Court's guide says 'Reserve has no legal meaning' for California.

AOP (Appellation d'origine protégée) is a product whose production steps are all carried out according to recognized know-how in one geographic area. It is a European sign that protects the name across the EU.
AOC (appellation d'origine contrôlée) is the mandatory national recognition step before a name is registered as an AOP. Only wine products keep the right to use the AOC term if they wish.
AOP rules are written in a cahier des charges defined by producers and approved by the EU, and checked by an independent body approved by INAO.

IGP identifies a product whose quality, reputation or other traits are linked to its geographic origin. At least one step of production must happen in the area; for wine, every operation from grape harvest to the end of winemaking happens in the zone.
INAO has been at the heart of French origin policy since 1935.
Italian law 238/2016, art. 28: DOP wines are classified as DOCG and DOC; IGP wines use the Italian term IGT. The Italian and EU terms may appear alone or together on the label.

Art. 33: DOCG is reserved for wines already DOC for at least seven years, judged of particular merit; DOC is reserved for wines from zones recognized as IGT for at least five years. A DOCG must have stricter rules than its DOC.
Art. 31: 'Classico' is for the oldest zone of origin (e.g. Chianti Classico). 'Riserva' needs at least two years of aging for reds and one year for whites.
Art. 31: 'Superiore' needs at least 10% lower yield per hectare and at least 0.5% more alcohol than the base wine. 'Gran Selezione' is only for DOCG wines made from the bottling estate's own grapes.
Art. 31: DO wines must show the vintage on the label, except fortified (liquorosi), non-vintage sparkling and frizzante wines.
Court guide for Piedmont lists the classification as IGP, DOC, DOCG, and label terms Normale and Riserva.
Spain (Ley 6/2015): 'Vino de la Tierra' marks an IGP wine; 'Vino de calidad de' marks a DOP wine.
'Denominación de origen' needs high commercial prestige and a region recognized as a quality wine with geographical indication for at least five years.
'Denominación de origen calificada' needs, on top of DO rules, at least 10 years using the term DO, and sale only in bottle from registered wineries inside the zone.
'Vino de pago' is a DOP from a 'pago': a rural site with its own soil and microclimate, known by a name tied to vine growing. All grapes must come from vineyards in the pago.

National aging terms for red DOP wines: Crianza at least 24 months with at least 6 in oak barrels of up to 330 liters; Reserva 36 months with at least 12 in oak; Gran Reserva 60 months with at least 18 in oak.

Rioja red: Crianza at least two years with at least one year in 225-liter oak barrels; Reserva at least three years with at least one in oak and six months in bottle; Gran Reserva at least five years with two in oak and two in bottle.
Court guide: Rioja is a DOCa. Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva are aging tiers in ascending order of minimum time; knowing the actual times is not necessary at the Introductory level.

Court guide, Germany: wine without geographic indication is Deutscher Wein; with GI: Landwein (regional), Qualitätswein (from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete) and Prädikatswein (a subset of Qualitätswein graded by ripeness at harvest). Chaptalization is not allowed for Prädikatswein.

The six Prädikate in order of ripeness: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein (same ripeness level as Beerenauslese), Trockenbeerenauslese. Kabinett and Spätlese are off-dry in style and can be made trocken; Beerenauslese and TBA are very sweet.
Ripeness at harvest sets the Prädikat, but choices in the winery decide how sweet the finished wine is.

VDP is a German producers' association with its own Burgundy-style vineyard classification. Grosses Gewächs: single-vineyard grand cru wines; Erstes Gewächs: premier cru. Label terms: Trocken = dry, Halbtrocken = half-dry.
The 1971 German Wine Law made ripeness at harvest the main measure of quality.
Eiswein is made from grapes as ripe as BA, harvested at minus 7°C or colder and pressed while frozen. Prädikat wines may not be enriched (chaptalized); Qualitätswein may.
Prädikatswein and Qualitätswein must come 100% from one of the 13 German growing regions and pass the quality test.
Since 1971 every Qualität and Prädikat wine has been lab-tested and sensory-tested and gets an official approval number shown on the label.

From 2021 Germany has an origin pyramid for Qualität and Prädikat wines, 'the smaller the origin, the higher the quality': single-vineyard wines (Großes Gewächs, Erstes Gewächs, other sites) at the top, then village wines (Ortswein), region wines, then the wine-growing area.
Under the 2021 rules, the term Qualitätswein can be replaced on all Qualität and Prädikat wines by 'wine with a protected designation of origin' plus the region name.
Großes Gewächs must be dry (trocken), hand-harvested, from a single vineyard, with the vintage on the label.
An American viticultural area (AVA) is a defined grape-growing region with a name, distinguishing features and a delineated boundary set in 27 CFR part 9.
US appellation rules: at least 75% from the named country, state or county; at least 85% from grapes grown in a named viticultural area. Imported wines follow the same 75% and 85% thresholds.
An appellation is required on the label when the wine shows a vintage date, a varietal name, a semi-generic name, 'estate bottled' and some other designations.

A single grape variety may be named if at least 75% of the wine is that variety, all grown in the labeled appellation. Vitis labrusca varieties may use 51% with a 'contains not less than 51%' statement.
Two or more varieties may be named only if all the grapes are those varieties and each percentage is shown on the label.
A wine may use a viticultural area name if at least 85% comes from grapes grown inside the AVA and, for US wine, it is fully finished in the state where the AVA lies.
Vintage: with an AVA appellation at least 95% of the wine must come from grapes harvested that year; with any other appellation, at least 85%.
'Estate bottled' requires an AVA appellation; the winery must be in the AVA, grow all the grapes on land it owns or controls there, and crush, ferment, age and bottle in a continuous process.
A vineyard, orchard, farm or ranch name may not appear unless 95% of the wine comes from that named place.

Court guide, California: 75% minimum grape variety, 85% minimum for AVA, 95% minimum for vintage, 95% for single vineyard, 100% for estate bottling. Reserve has no legal meaning; Meritage is a trademark.
Court guide, Catalonia: Priorat is a DOCa; Cava is a DO.
Court guide, Oregon: 90% minimum for stated variety (with exceptions such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) and 95% minimum for AVA.

unverified: EU varietal and vintage minimums (Wine Folly gives 85% for France, Italy, Germany and others): the EU regulation (2019/33, art. 50) could not be fetched, so no European percentage is stated as fact.

Vin de France (France's wine without geographic indication) and Italy's equivalent tier were not confirmed on an official page fetched, so the intro band only lists Germany's Deutscher Wein for that tier.
Court guide says '95% minimum for vintage' for California without the federal split; TTB rule (27 CFR 4.27) is 95% only with an AVA and 85% with other appellations. The chapter follows TTB.
Court guide says '100% for Estate Bottling; must be in the same county'. The federal rule fetched (27 CFR 4.26) ties estate bottling to an AVA, not a county; the county wording was not confirmed.
Oregon's 90%/95% rules come from the Court guide and Wine Folly only; Oregon's own regulations were not fetched.
German minimum must weights conflict between Wines of Germany pages (one says Eiswein and BA need 120°Oe; another gives 110–128°Oe by region), so no Oechsle figures are used.
The 2021 German origin pyramid allowed a transition for older labeling through the 2025 harvest; how labels look from the 2026 vintage was not checked.
The Italian law text used is the Lazio agency (ARSIAL) copy of Law 238/2016 as published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale (Vigente al 12-1-2017); later amendments were not checked.
Germany's Landwein is listed by the Court as a wine 'with geographic indication', but no official page fetched confirms it as the EU PGI tier, so it is left out of the PGI row.
